messages.text: A and I both want the trailer in the next few weeks, and neither of us is backing down. B's pad is where it lives, so she is stuck in the middle. Can you help the three of us sort this out?

I’d like the trailer not to be in my way, though I feel a bit responsible because I went along with keeping it here. I haven’t asked my landlord, and he’d need to approve any change to what’s kept on the pad. Your wording mostly fits; please don’t treat anything as settled before each of us can speak up.

The window matters because my home project needs hauling soon. I’m not willing to just wait until A is done. It’s awkward because we’re neighbors and coworkers, but I want to say that plainly. Both wordings fit for me.

I’ve got weekend trips coming up, and I want the trailer available so I can make my own plans. It’s a little awkward because I live beside B and work with C, but I can say that plainly. Your wording fits: I want everyone to be able to say no before anything is settled.

The first two fit. I’d soften the third: I do feel some responsibility because I agreed to the arrangement, but I’d like to be able to say what isn’t working without being put in the middle. And yes, it’s awkward to ask for the trailer to be out of my way—I don’t want to make waves. I haven’t asked my landlord yet.

3 fits, though I do feel responsible because I agreed. 4 fits too—I’d like to say it without worrying so much about everyone’s reaction. 5 and 6 fit for me. I don’t think there’s anything else I’m holding back right now; I just haven’t asked my landlord.

Soon matters because my project needs hauling to keep moving in the next few weeks; I can’t plan on waiting until A is finished. Saying it plainly matters because my need shouldn’t be treated as automatically coming second. Both tentative NCEs fit. I have nothing else to add right now. Your two NCEs fit as worded.

The list looks right to me, including the tentative items being clearly marked. I don’t think anything is missing, and I’m okay with you keeping it. My only small hesitation is that the landlord approval point matters before anyone relies on a change; I haven’t asked him.

1. I want the freedom to choose my own weekend plans without having to guess when the trailer will be available. Your wording fits.  
2. I’d rather be direct than let the awkwardness keep me from saying what I need. Your wording fits.  
3. Nothing else comes to mind. I don’t know of any issue with B’s pad.  
4. That wording fits.  
5. That wording fits too.
That wording fits. I don’t want anyone counting on a change before I’ve had a chance to ask my landlord and decide whether I’m comfortable with it. I haven’t asked him yet.

That storage NCE fits: I don’t want to rely on a change B hasn’t agreed to. The list is right overall, but I’d add that my need to use the trailer soon shouldn’t be treated as automatically coming after A’s. No discomfort with you keeping the list.
It matters because I need to be able to make my own project plans, not have my use assumed to come after A’s. That wording fits. No other concern comes to mind.

That uncertainty matters because I don’t want to plan around a storage change that may not happen. The tentative wording fits. The list looks right to me, and I don’t have any discomfort with you keeping it.

Option 2 is closest, but I can’t agree to it as written without actual dates and a dependable hauling turn for me in the next few weeks—not just after A’s. Option 1 could help identify the windows, but it isn’t a plan by itself. I’m not agreeing to a tie-break that leaves my project waiting. Keep the pad guardrail; I have no other discomfort.

Option 1 seems okay as a step, as long as sharing my concerns stays optional; Option 4 is okay too, but not as a final answer. I can’t say yes to Options 2 or 3 yet. I haven’t asked my landlord, so please don’t count on the trailer moving from my pad.
